subject: chemistry_2
question_text: The two strands in DNA are not identical, but are complementary. Explain.

verification.note: Unit 13 (Biomolecules) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 10 "BIOMOLECULES", book pp.99-104; the book prints this question on book p.102 as SAQ 7. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK SPELLING: the printed question reads "complimentary"; the word is complementary, and it is written correctly in question_text. CROSS-SUBJECT: Junior Botany's ts_ipe_b1_bm_nucleic_acid_secondary_structure covers the same double helix and the same A=T two-bond, G≡C three-bond rule. This card uses the same numbers and the same pairing, so the two banks agree; the botany card treats the helix as an example of secondary structure, while this one answers the identical-versus-complementary question.

steps.label: The double helix
lines: DNA is a double helix. Two polynucleotide
strands coil around one common axis.
The sugar and phosphate groups form the
backbone on the outside of the helix.
The nitrogenous bases point inwards, and
the two strands are held together by
hydrogen bonds between them.
steps.why: The bases face each other across the axis, so each base on one strand is opposite a base on the other, and it is that facing arrangement which makes a pairing rule possible at all. The backbone stays on the outside and takes no part in the pairing.
common_mistakes: Writing that the two strands are held by covalent bonds. They are held by hydrogen bonds between the bases.
Placing the bases on the outside. The bases point inwards; the sugar-phosphate backbone is outside.
steps.memory_tip: Backbone outside, bases inside, facing each other across the axis.
steps.margin_note: Set the structure up first. The pairing rule makes no sense until the bases are shown facing each other.

steps.label: The pairing rule
lines: The pairing between the two strands is
fixed:
A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so
every base pair is the same size and the
helix keeps a constant width.
steps.why: The rule is not a preference but a consequence of size and of where the hydrogen-bonding groups sit: only these two combinations fit the space and match up their donors and acceptors. Pairing a large purine with a small pyrimidine every time is what keeps the width of the helix constant.
common_mistakes: Writing that adenine pairs with guanine. Both are purines and two purines are too wide to fit.
Writing that the pairing is random. It is fixed: A with T, and G with C.
steps.memory_tip: A with T, G with C. Always one big base with one small base.
steps.margin_note: Write the two pairs as two separate lines. That layout is what the examiner scans for.

steps.label: The hydrogen bonds
lines: The number of hydrogen bonds in each pair
is fixed as well:
The number is set by how many bonding
groups the two bases can offer each other.
A G–C rich region is therefore harder to
separate than an A–T rich region.
steps.why: Two and three are fixed numbers, not approximations, and they are worth a mark on their own. They also have a consequence: three bonds hold more strongly than two, so a stretch rich in G and C needs more heat to separate the strands.
common_mistakes: Giving three hydrogen bonds to A–T and two to G–C. It is the other way round: A=T has two, G≡C has three.
Writing that all base pairs are held by the same number of bonds. The two pairs differ.
steps.memory_tip: A=T is a double line, G≡C is a triple line. Two and three.
steps.margin_note: These two numbers are a whole mark and take one line. Never leave them out.

steps.label: What complementary means

lines.text: Opposite A is T; opposite G is C

lines: So the two strands are not copies of each
other: they are not identical.
The order of bases on one strand fixes the
order on the other strand completely.
That is what complementary means, and it is
how DNA is able to copy itself.
steps.why: The question is asking for the difference between identical and complementary, so the answer has to end by naming it. Identical would mean the same sequence on both strands; complementary means each base is matched by the one base that fits it, so one strand is enough to reconstruct the other.
common_mistakes: Writing that the two strands have the same base sequence. They have matched sequences, not the same one.
Explaining the pairing and never using the word complementary. The question asks what the word means.
steps.memory_tip: Not the same strand twice; each one is the pattern for the other.
steps.margin_note: Answer the actual question in the last two lines: complementary, not identical.

insider_note: Four steps: helix, pairing rule, bond counts, meaning. The last step is the one that answers the question as asked, so leave room for it.
